speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, with a motion to proceed without formalities and be read a first time, which was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The speech introduced bills to implement the Montreal Convention for international air carrier liability, strengthen Customs border enforcement and search powers, modernise customs procedures, define tobacco content for duty, and amend the Export Market Development Grants scheme. Key changes include removing the air liability cap with claims up to 100,000 SDR (about A$172,000), and raising the EMDG maximum grant to $200,000, the turnover limit to $50 million, and lowering the expenditure threshold to $10,000.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The opposition moved to refer several government bills to Senate committees for extended inquiry, arguing they required careful scrutiny and were not election policies. The government accused the opposition of economic vandalism, claiming the delays would cost up to $284 million and undermine the budget surplus strategy.
The debate resumed on the luxury car tax bills, with an amendment moved by Senators Bartlett and Nettle to require passage by 24 June 2008 and to omit paragraph (2) of the motion.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the opposition is delaying eight bills through Senate committee referrals without proper justification, including the Same-Sex Relationships (Superannuation) Bill 2008 and the Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Political Donations and Other Measures) Bill 2008. The speaker urged the opposition to support the same‑sex superannuation bill by 1 July, and to pass electoral reforms lowering the donation disclosure threshold to $1,000, banning overseas and anonymous donations, and preventing parties from profiting from public funding.

speeches.speaker: Kerry O'Brien
speeches.brief: The report of the Standing Committee on Economics on the Tax Laws Amendment (Luxury Car Tax) Bill 2008 and three related bills was presented to the Senate and ordered to be printed.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The opposition argued the luxury car tax increase is bad policy because it is inflationary, inequitable, and harmful to the Australian car manufacturing sector, noting that 12% of vehicles are now covered compared to 2.5% when the tax was introduced. The speaker opposed the tax's retrospectivity and claimed it unfairly impacts rural and tourism industries, with the most commonly affected vehicle being the Toyota LandCruiser, not high-end luxury cars.

speeches.speaker: Annette Hurley
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of increasing the luxury car tax from 25% to 33%, stating it would only affect vehicles priced above $57,180 and would have a negligible 0.01% one-off impact on inflation. The speaker rejected opposition claims that the tax would harm large families, people with disabilities, or rural communities, citing specific vehicle prices and exemptions for commercial vehicles, emergency vehicles, and disability-modified cars.

speeches.speaker: David Bushby
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Tax Laws Amendment (Luxury Car Tax) Bill 2008, arguing that increasing the tax from 25% to 33% on vehicles over $57,180 would harm rural and regional Australians, small tourism businesses, and the local car industry, particularly affecting vehicles like the Toyota LandCruiser and Ford Territory. The speaker also criticised a reported deal with the Greens to exempt 24 imported fuel-efficient cars up to $75,000 while taxing Australian-made models, and raised concerns that the tax would be inflationary rather than deflationary.

speeches.speaker: Jan McLucas
speeches.brief: The government increased the luxury car tax from 25% to 33% from 1 July 2008 to raise over $500 million over four years, contributing to a $21.7 billion surplus. Amendments were introduced to exempt fuel-efficient cars (under 7 litres per 100km) from the higher rate, and the Treasurer referred the Greens' proposal to phase out the tax to the Henry tax review.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The speaker sought and obtained leave to recommit the votes on the second reading of the Tax Laws Amendment (Luxury Car Tax) Bill 2008 and related bills, after which the question was put that the bills be read a second time.

speeches.speaker: Mark Bishop
speeches.brief: The vote on the Tax Laws Amendment (Luxury Car Tax) Bill 2008 and related bills resulted in 34 ayes and 34 noes, so the matter was lost.

speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The opposition argued the luxury car tax increase from 25% to 33% is a punitive "tax grab" that will harm Australian car manufacturers and cost jobs, particularly in South Australia and Victoria. They stated the tax is inflationary, unfairly targets rural and regional Australians who rely on four-wheel drives like the Toyota LandCruiser, and that the government's amendments only provide narrow exemptions for primary producers and tourism operators while excluding many others.
The Tax Laws Amendment (Luxury Car Tax) Bill 2008 and related bills were debated, with Senator Sherry moving that they be read a second time.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the luxury car tax increase, arguing it would harm Australian manufacturing workers and rural families, and proposed a two-tier amendment keeping the 25% tax on cars up to $90,000 and applying 33% above that.
Senator Sherry moved the second reading of four bills amending the luxury car tax.

speeches.speaker: Ron Boswell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against the proposed luxury car tax, stating it would unfairly harm rural Australians, Aboriginal communities, boat and caravan industries, and Australian car manufacturers like Toyota, Nissan, and Mitsubishi, while exempting expensive European cars. The speaker supported an amendment from Senator Fielding to exempt farmers and tourism operators, but called for broader exemptions for all remote area workers.
